title: Insect Cosmeceuticals—Because You’re Worth It?
content: The “snake oil salesman” is a colorful figure from our nation’s past, part of our rich tradition of false advertising aimed at separating unsophisticated customers from their hard-earned money. Today, the term is a metaphor for anyone who uses deception, hype, or outright lies for profit—that is, a cheat or swindler who sells worthless products by making extravagant and completely unsupportable claims. The metaphor owes its origins to the literal sellers of “snake oil” in the United States in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In Asia, oil pressed from snakes, particularly the Chinese water snake Laticauda semifasciata (a.k.a. black-banded sea krait; Haynes 2015) evidently has had a place in pharmacopoeias for at least two millennia (Zhou and Jiang 2004), and when Chinese immigrants began to arrive in the United States in large numbers for work opportunities in the 19th century, they brought their traditions, including an abiding belief in the curative powers of snake oils, with them.
